utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just, Mr. Lukic, please don't intervene when I'm having a discussion with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is all clear to me. You are completely right. The law says what it says; that is clear. However, that does not qualify the MUP staff as an organizational unit due to everything we've discussed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a legal principle in the -- or was there at the time, in 1999 -- sorry, we're talking about -- yeah, 1998, say, was there a legal principle in Serbia that there -- it's presumed that in a properly organized administration things are done properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such a principle applied the way you defined it did not exist. However, one can draw a conclusion as to the intention, the idea was in place in terms of organising the administration and this is one of the elementary principles of administrations. There were articles referring to that situation. However, you pin-pointed this exactly. It is a legal shortcoming. As a lawyer, I cannot dispute that. However, the fact of this person's sent to that place does not make that body an organizational unit. The mere act of deploying that person there does not make it so, and this can be seen from the wartime [as interpreted] record of Mr. Lukic and everything that we are about to look into, but you are correct. I hand it to you, you pin-pointed it directly, it was a mistake, a gap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, where are we in your examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Close to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, we need to have a break at this stage. While we have that break could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will resume in half an hour and that will be at 20 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we continue, I just want to make one correction. Transcript page 48, line 2, it's recorded wartime record of Mr. Lukic, and expert said work record of Mr. Lukic or work book record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, may we continue?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 72 that we discussed, does it describe and define organizational units as opposed to units which are not organizational units?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what is the main purpose of this article.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the beauty of the legal science. We can try and interpret this article so as to try and get to the gist of it. The basic idea of the article is for the ministry, or rather, the administrations of any given ministry can send their employees to other posts within the same ministry without their consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That will suffice. Let us please have 6D1360 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We sent the translation of this document this morning, but it's not in the system yet but the Prosecution should have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, since as you usually like to say, are you following me, I'm going to ask the same.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am following.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is this about?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a work record, work log. It doesn't say who it belongs to, but we have the unique identification number, based on that we can see who it belongs to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 3 of the document -- page 2, first, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see who it belongs to?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This page reveals that this workbook belongs to Sreten Lukic. We see his level of education, place of birth, and on the right-hand we see the exams passed and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go to page 3 next. I would like you to tell us the following. The two entries in the middle, 7052 and 2243, what do these refer to?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It tells us a lot. Let us try and clear up a few things. To me as a lawyer this is crystal clear. The middle entry it says the title and seat of company or institution at which one is employed. We can see that this person worked with the SUP of Belgrade as of the 1st of August. I can't tell what year it is exactly, I think it's 1987, the 1st of August, right. And then the last date is when the employment ceased. We can see here what organizational unit the aforementioned person worked in, that is, where the person began working, where the person was when he ended working, et cetera, et cetera. It applies across Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about 2243?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entry 2243 it says that the aforementioned person began working with the SUP of Belgrade of the MUP of Serbia. The date, the 1st of January, 1992, the employment ceased on the 15th of July, 1999. The person worked with the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade within this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the last entry?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, the 15th of July, 1999. This means that on that date the person started working with that unit, that is, the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia. Therefore, he meant from the city of Belgrade SUP to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems obvious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, please continue, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this work record there is no mention of the MUP staff. What does that tell you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That shows that the person was sent to the MUP staff and that it exercised its work duties and obligation in the or with the organizational unit he was sent from. He was a SUP Belgrade worker during the year when he was there. This is in keeping with the Law on Labour Relations and State Bodies. May I explain one thing further so as not to waste any time later. If we look at the work record of a person employed with the SAJ, then we would be able to see under name and seat of the organization it would read SAJ since it was an organizational unit as well as with the dates when the employment began and ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Professor, does this document mean that Mr. Lukic is still engaged by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, formally, legally speaking, the date of employment was the 15th of July, 1999, and there is no date in the last column. Legally speaking, we come across the problem we encountered before, and that is the imperfection of the work of the administration. First of all, it is not possible that he's still employed because he's been outside the MUP for a number of years and there must be a decision on the termination of his employment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could another explanation be that this is -- that had been photocopied before his employment was terminated?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, sir, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you researched the question whether he's still engaged by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have not researched that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I am certain that he is no longer a MUP employ. It is not possible and I believe it is indisputable. This was probably copied before the last entry was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So would there have to be a decision terminating his engagement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely so, in keeping with the rules and the law, such a decision should exist. It was probably in existence but it is not recorded here since this is just a photocopy. I'm quite sure that in the original work record you have that but we can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things that your report says is that when a person leaves the service of the MUP he is no longer entitled to use his rank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is absolutely correct, that is in keeping with the Law on Ranks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Virtually everyone here calls him General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour, you are quite right. He is no longer a general. In keeping with the Law on -- well, there are two laws here, one on the rank and the other on the function. Once a person terminates his employment, that person no longer has the right to use the rank, it is not the army where you can retain your rank, but right now he's an ordinary citizen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. The fact that it happens, though, led to me asking the question whether perhaps he is still engaged by the MUP and therefore entitled to that rank --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe you noticed, Your Honour, that I always address him Mr. Lukic. Only when we talk about that time when something has to be clarified we say "general," maybe people wouldn't know who -- there are many Lukics, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, Professor, is it customary and do you know on the basis of what provisional bodies, commissions, are established within state organs, within the state administration?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. A possibility is envisaged within state administration organs to establish provisional bodies, temporary bodies. When speaking about such bodies and commissions that are established within the Ministry of the Interior, they are envisaged in Article 11 of the rules on the internal organization of the Ministry of the Interior. I am sorry, Article 10. In Article 10 it says that the chief of the department or the chief of the secretariat can establish standing or provisional staffs, commissions, working groups, and other working bodies within the ministry or department in order to look into certain matters from the line of work of the department and also, when necessary, in order to carry out certain complex tasks so required to be carried out by people who are specialised in particular organizational units."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there is this possibility and also within other state organs too?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that was the idea, to have the state administration be as flexible as possible so that they can resolve different tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see that the MUP staff in Pristina had the authority to appoint policemen in Kosovo and Metohija, or rather, deploy them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP staff in Pristina did not have the right to appoint or deploy policemen in Kosovo; that is to say they did not have the legal possibility of changing one's employment status because that fell under the purview of the organizational units involved. When we're talking about the secretariat we're talking about the chief of secretariat; when we're talking about the MUP, then the level is the chief of department -- well, there are different variants but this would be my basic answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's -- this isn't the basis you -- or are you saying this is the basis for the establishment of the MUP staff? You're not saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Your Honour, are you asking me this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. This is a provision that you say deals with the appointment of ad hoc bodies, working groups, commissions. Now, are you suggesting that that's the proper basis, legal basis, for the establishment of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the way it is. The MUP staff was not based on this article. Other articles were invoked; however, other bodies were based on this article because it was the chief of the department that had established them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where are we going on this in relation to the MUP staff, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, Article 43, paragraph 1, from Article 69 of the Law on State Administration.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 7 of the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see that that is mentioned as the basis for the establishment of the staff dated the 16th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, well this is the way it was. When -- well, how shall I put this? The staff -- well, a body that did not have the status of an organizational unit, then -- then -- then he invoked the Law on State Administration, which gives the minister the right to be in charge of the work of a specific ministry, that is to say to make decisions that have to do with carrying out particular affairs within that ministry, and then also he invoked Article 7 on the Law on Internal Affairs that says: "The minister prescribes the way in which work will be carried out within the Ministry of the Interior and provides instructions as to how this work is to be carried out." So this is all the work that has to do with some other matters that go beyond the organizational units. As a legal line we have Articles 23 of the Law on Ministries and Article 43 on the Law on State Administration which authorises the minister to do that. If necessary we can analyse these articles or whatever you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, start again, please, you overlapped with the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the time being I don't want to go into it any further unless Your Honour wants the Professor to explain these provisions further.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not necessary if Mr. Lukic does not want to explore it. I'm perfectly capable of reading articles for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you looked at the documentation did you form an opinion of your own as to whether the MUP staff in Pristina had the authority to discipline any policeman in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No dilemma about that because the system of disciplinary punishment is in its basic elements regulated by the Law on Internal Affairs, and it is spelled out more specifically in the decree on disciplinary responsibility of persons employed in the ministry. Then there is another line involved and that is -- there is another instruction, rather -- or rather, there is another solution -- or rather, a document, we look at it yesterday, it regulates this question in a situation when there is a state of war --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter does not hear Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is clearly defined. It is clear that the leader of the organizational unit can, can, as a first-instance decision prescribe a sanction -- or rather, mete out disciplinary punishment for less- or more-serious infractions within his organizational unit. The second-instance is different, that involves a disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The only problem I have with your answer is that you said that you looked at that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, sorry, I mean I'm totally -- well, yeah. This is something that is so well-known to me because I've been dealing with the analysis of these legal norms for months now, so it's all so clear to me and these are general matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, 6D464. What we have here is a document in which the chief of the secretariat in Pristina addresses the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, the police administration chief, for their approval to have a misdemeanour report filed against a policeman. In your work did you come across such a case that the MUP staff could ask for approval to file a misdemeanour report against any policeman in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to that question is perfectly clear because all of these questions have to do with establishing responsibility for starting disciplinary proceedings and within the system of organizational units -- well, that is where it was. So it is only the head of an organizational unit that can propose the initiation of such proceedings as far as disciplinary responsibility is concerned. As for misdemeanours and that responsibility, for a while there was a rule that was in force in Serbia that the head of an organizational unit has to send a request that was called approval along the line of work within the ministry to file a misdemeanour report or a criminal report. The underlying idea of this document that did perhaps have this clumsy title was that -- it wasn't that the ministry was supposed to give its approval or not give its approval. The idea as carried through in practice meant that within the ministry there should be a uniform system of information with regard to persons from this system of the ministry that had committed crimes, misdemeanours, or disciplinary infractions. Approval was always given, absolutely, it was always allowed. In this specific case the chief of the secretariat would file a request to have misdemeanour proceedings initiated before the court that it has jurisdiction from the point of view of a territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the MUP staff provide this kind of approval -- just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's for sure, no, it couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 6D1339, please. The next document has not been translated, but I can ask you even without that whether the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija could ask approval for starting criminal proceedings, for filing a criminal report, rather, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation is absolutely the same as in the case of misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're getting close to the end. 1D680, could that please be called up. We're going to need page 2 in both versions, please. Professor, what we have before us is a proposal of the minister of the interior to the president of the Republic of Serbia to promote Mr. Sreten Lukic. Could you please tell us whether this document shows whether this is a regular promotion or an extraordinary promotion, fast-track promotion, and on the basis of what regulations can this be seen?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's clear. In the first paragraph of this document the minister invokes Article 6 of the Law on Ranks of the Ministry of the Interior. Article 6 of the law envisages regular promotions. In Articles 7 and 8 certain requirements are stated, and Article 10 provides for extraordinary promotions, so it is not Article 10, it is Article 6 that is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you characterize the document that is written for regular promotions? Is it a constituent or a declarative document?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as this kind of a document is concerned, well, it is a document which, in fact -- well, conditionally speaking, it is hard to distinguish this way but to have certain conditions met in the view of the minister that a particular person had met the requirements for regular promotion in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question that His Honour Judge Bonomy insisted upon as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move to that, you will see the final paragraph of that document which referred to Mr. Lukic excelling in successful command and control of the MUP units engaged in the prevention of terrorism in Kosovo. Can you tell us which MUP units these were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the translation. Here it is. It's clear, Your Honour. The question is quite proper. The arguments presented in paragraph 3 really do not hold water. That is the difference between what exists in practice and what is written. As I've explained so far, he could not engage in command and control. This is a brilliant example of what formalism means in law without a base, without grounds, without a foundation. Your Honours, I'm sure as a lawyer and a person who tries to see beyond that and to see organization -- maybe this was the 13th of May or some other occasion or on account of the bombing, but he could not engage in command and control in view of the system. That is what is quite clear within that system. We can adopt any norm whatsoever, but if it's not part of the system, if it cannot live in that context, then it is just a letter on paper and that is so clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in light of that were you able to establish why in fact he was promoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of studying this document it is more than clear that this is a regular promotion, it is not an extraordinary promotion. Now, why he was promoted, the 13th of May, this is an appropriate occasion, the 13th of May. So the proposal was made on the 11th of May, 1999, when the bombing of Serbia was underway. I was in Serbia at the time, and every week they promoted say 50 people every week and this was on television. It was ridiculous to me. That shows to me a state that does not have a strength of its own and then it gives decorations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But these are -- this is a regular promotion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, regular in his case, but I'm telling you there were a lot of documents, officers -- generals, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please slow down. And, Mr. Lukic, this is the last time I will warn you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm so sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- this is the last time I will warn you not to interfere when I am asking questions of a witness and getting answers from him. It's happened three times in the course of this evidence alone. Now, what I'm trying to understand here is why a letter has a justification for promotion. Now, are you saying you don't need a justification to promote somebody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document would have been perfect from a legal point of view had it only contained the first paragraph in accordance with the law and regular proceedings and by an authorised official in terms of proposals such as the minister is. That would have been perfect from a legal point of view and it would have been sufficient. The third paragraph shouldn't have been there, speaking from a legal point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in your opinion why is the third paragraph there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean -- I think it's superfluous and incorrect. My entire expertise and my appearance before this Court has been an attempt to explanation this organization that he could not exercise command and control over units of the Ministry of the Interior because this was a different system, a different line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question is simple: Why in your opinion is it there? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could not explain -- I cannot give a rational reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour. I was on my feet, so I was under the impression that I am leading the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Professor, we have another area to get through, and His Honour Judge Bonomy mentioned this at the beginning. In your opinion, what did the staff do, the staff of MUP, in Kosovo and Metohija? In reviewing the documents and listening to certain testimony did you gain an impression of that? Did you come to a conclusion? Which tasks did the staff in Kosovo and Metohija actually perform? And that would be my last question.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of everything that I studied thus far, the legal norms, the system itself, the individual decisions and I came across and the documents that I looked at and so on and so forth, it is without a doubt that that staff of the MUP within the system as far as I'm concerned could undertake a process of informing vertically upwards and downwards during a period of time, and that was because it was introduced into the system of informing, having in mind the document we studied yesterday. So that was the only systemic line or chain where it could have functioned within that framework. Outside that, realistically viewed, it could have been an auxiliary body dealing with logistics, for example, or training or things like that, some sort of communication. But it could not have been in the system of control and command and planning because those were other systems, other lines, other chains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. That would be all as far as my Defence team is concerned.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Professor, do I rightly understand that these are things you say it could have done but you haven't studied what it actually did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what the MUP staff - we're talking about the MUP staff, not the MUP itself, the MUP staff we're talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because those are two different things. Well, on the basis of an analysis of the documents and the system, I'm absolutely certain that within the frameworks of that particular system the MUP staff could only have been within the area of information, bearing in mind the decision we looked at yesterday about flank information and what we could explain. But it wasn't in the system. When I say that I mean planning, I mean management, I mean organization, and everything set out in that decision pursuant to establishment, whereas the system as a whole did not change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination by any Defence counsel? You will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just ask you a little bit about yourself, Professor. In 1999 where were you working at? I can't make out exactly where you were from your CV.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in the course of 1999, that period, I was employed at the Faculty of Law in Kragujevac as a professor on the subject of crime, criminal science. Now, in 1999 as well I was professor of criminal science at the Faculty of Law in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that -- during the war period I went to Belgrade to hold classes there because tuition was ongoing during that time and so were the examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever worked in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never an employee of the MUP; however, I worked on several projects after the changes in Serbia took place, which is after 2000, which had to do with police reform. So I'm one of the founders of community policy [as interpreted] in Serbia. I wrote a book about that, I was member of certain commissions working on the project in my own town, the town of Kragujevac, and I was one of the leaders of that project.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a -- I think a transcript or translation issue at page 17, line 13, I believe he said community policing not policy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Community policing, yes, that's your term and your model and you're well-acquainted with that, I believe. It's a different concept for the police than it was in 1998 and 1999. So the police in Serbia is trying to change, and I had a part to play in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I see or I saw from your CV that you have published in the area of what you call criminalistics and criminal trials especially interviews of accused. Prior to preparing this report did you publish any work in respect to the structure and organization of the MUP in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wrote about the organization of the police within the frameworks of my book, in my book, where I deal with the problem of community policing and support work to that book. And within that the organization of MUP, both in Serbia and Kosovo and the other states of the former Yugoslavia and further afield in the world as well in order to try and draw certain conclusions and make certain proposals. So the answer is I dealt with the problem of the organization of policing in Kosovo, organization illegally [as interpreted] and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P1505.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to correct this one as well, 66, 10, says organizationally, legally, and so on. He definitely didn't say illegally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say illegally, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, your last answer says, but your CV doesn't disclose this, that you dealt with the problem of the organization of policing in Kosovo. Have you dealt with that specifically as a separate matter or do you mean simply that you've dealt with policing in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I dealt with that within the frameworks of police work in Serbia, that is to say this police work in Serbia at the time ran along the same principles throughout the territory of Serbia, the same laws applied, the same rules applied, the same system of organization and responsibility. There was no difference, and that is something I dealt with, bearing in mind the knowledge that was necessary to promote the police to, introduce the community policing system as it exists elsewhere in the world. So I looked at its implementation through the projects that I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do we have 1505?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while we're looking at it, I'd like to go to the part of the report where you deal with it specifically, that is page 85 in English, I think that's page 149 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page did you say in Serbian, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I must confess that when I read this paragraph I did not understand you to be saying that this order of the minister, P1505, was an order that was impossible to implement, as you have put it here today or yesterday, what you described as a mission impossible. Indeed, without reading everything you said about it on that page, I --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- will just read one part and ask you a question. This is the first paragraph of page 85 in English, and the penultimate sentence reads: "Also, there was a provision which enabled the head of the staff to request that other ministry employees be assigned to the staff. Such assignment was possible pursuant to Article 72 of the Law on Internal Affairs. These illegal provisions made it impossible to assign employees to duties from one organization of unit in the Ministry of the Interior to another in any part of the Republic of Serbia. So this was not a unique or special option. These were regular options envisaged by the Law on Internal Affairs." And the proceeding sentences in that paragraph led me to the view that you're saying that this order that you have before you, 1505, was not impossible to implement but was, in fact, implemented. So I would ask you first: Did you in your report say that order 1505 was impossible to implement and where, if so, did you say so?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you wish me to answer now? The entire analysis of this document in a way leads to that conclusion; however, on page, for example, 149 in the Serbian version, paragraph 3, paragraph 3 of that page, says the following. And we're talking about the decision by which the staff was established. It says: "The substance of this decision lies in the fact that none of the organizational units at the seat of the ministry in Belgrade, none of the regional secretariats of the interior in Kosovo and Metohija, and none of the organizational units attached to them of the ministry in Kosovo and Metohija did not lose with the formation of the staff any part of its competence and authorities." So it is clear from that that you can draw the conclusion that I made orally. That's right, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mean in saying that none of the organizational units lost any part of their responsibilities, it follows logically that the minister's order was, therefore, impossible to implement. Very well, that is your answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The following sentence after the part you just read: "The staff was only an admission to the already-existing organizational structure and horizontal and vertical lines of command established by the acts of internal organization of the ministry and the RDB in the ministry and not in any way a substitute that broke, changed, or altered internal organizational structures and lines of command. Professor, weren't you saying that the staff was an organizational form that complemented the structure that existed in Kosovo at the time; is that what you were saying in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but let's take it this way. The MUP staff was not an organizational unit and was not within the system, whereas the system existed outside the system defined by law and the rules and the norms emanating from the rules. Now, with the formation or -- with this decision not a single authorisation or duty or assignment of the other organizational units was taken away from them and handed over to the staff and they had to say that 100 per cent of the authority that the secretariat in Pristina had, for example, 10 per cent or 20 per cent is handed over to the MUP staff; MUP staff, no, that was not the case. What I'm certain of without entering into the system or what did not enter into the system was the dispatch of the alleged information of the MUP staff, but this takes nothing away from others in Kosovo, it just adds a new obligation because of certain strategic goals having to do with the question of analysis. So nothing was taken away from anybody. You can't say you have 100 per cent without taking away something from someone else, the system of rights, responsibilities, that's the problem, and that's why I say I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your answer, but when you say that the staff was an addition to the already-existing organizational structure and horizontal and vertical lines of command established by the acts on internal organization, what do you mean if not that the staff was complementing the structure that already existed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the staff was not complementary, it was outside that existing structure, like an auxiliary body, an addition, and that emanates from the entire system that was established by the rules governing the internal organization of -- for the area of internal affairs. So that must be clear to one and all. Law and legal matters depend on logic, it's mathematics, you can measure it, and that is why law is a science.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. In the previous page of your report of the English version here, you refer -- and this is page 84, first paragraph which deals with 6D1368, an order --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the page is in Serbian so that I'm able to follow, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph, which sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the paragraph -- it's one paragraph in that page I think -- or the first page of that page, 147 --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what's the sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's at footnote 441.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Footnote -- it's footnote 446 and 448 in my version, but I'll go back to 441. 441 is on page 146 of the Serbian, but I found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see, it goes from 146 to 147. And it refers to a decree on the establishment of the ministry staff in Kosovo on the 11th of June, 1999, which for the record is 6D1368. And --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you provide me with that document, please, I would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have 6D1368 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have I been given the document? Is it in front of me? Is this what I'm looking at? The 5th of April, 1996, that's what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on and it will appear before you on the screen in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I may have a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A copy will be printed, Mr. Stamp. Apparently there's a problem with e-court. Now you're ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have it there now? This is a decision establishing the MUP staff for Kosovo of the 5th of April, 1996 [sic].

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you look at paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in item 2 it says: "The task of the staff is to" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You don't need to read it. Just have a look at it and paragraph 3. In paragraph 3 it will indicate that it can issue orders and control the work in progress. And if you look at the end of it --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- you will see that this was issued by the assistant minister Djordjevic, the 11th of June, 1997. I'm sorry, if I said 1996 before.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And your question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One second. I'm sorry for interrupting just now, but I don't think that we have this number or the number is wrong, 6D1368 is not on the list of the exhibits we used with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Or -- well, even if it is not on the list it ought to have been on the list. This is a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a different matter, it ought to be. It's not on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's referred to in footnote 441 of the report that's presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Footnote 441 deals with another document -- oh, sorry, 441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 11th of June, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at the signature section of the document you will see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's in the report, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, this is -- this decree giving the MUP staff the status and these powers in 1996, are you also saying -- in 1997, I'm sorry - that this one was impossible to implement, a mission impossible?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question very well. I will try to provide you with an answer, a logical one, and I'll try to explain my view of the situation following the analysis I carried out. We are lawyers. There is no dilemma that each individual document needs to be implemented. The systemic regulation needs to be changed. It is one of the basic principles any legal system operates on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask you to pause here. We'll get to the explanations --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- and legal and scientific explanations shortly. But could you just tell me first if it is your opinion that this which has similar tasks to the order of June 1998 and similar powers to the order of June 1998 that you said were impossible to implement, if you also opine that this was also impossible to implement, the one before you now.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That document is an individual decision and it doesn't change the system. It was made by the chief of the sector, not the minister. The organization and functioning of the ministry is something that is regulated by the minister pursuant to various laws that I may refer you to. That means that no individual decision on the part of the chief of sector which is at the lower level than the minister could change the systemic document put into force by the minister, such as the rules, and it also needs to be approved by the government in keeping with the regulations I mentioned yesterday. It is a decree --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just want a simple answer to the question. I take it your answer is in respect to this order, the 11th of June, 1999 -- 1997, was also impossible to implement; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the times were different and it wasn't felt so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. In the next page, page 147 in Serbian and it's same page in English, page 84, you also deal with the next decree which renewed the -- or which re-established the ministry staff in Pristina, the decree of the 15th of May, 1998, and that is P1251. Is it possible to bring it up now? This is another decision of Assistant Minister Djordjevic. And if you look at the mandate or the task at page 2 -- at item 2 you'll see that it's pretty much similar to the later order of the minister in June, except that it now incorporates the suppression of terrorism. I just want to know, are you saying now that this order is also -- was also impossible to implement?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Prosecutor, this decision was made pursuant to Article 2 on the rules of internal organization. If we refer to Article 10, we see there that the minister of the chief of secretariat can establish individual certain bodies, commissions, or working groups in order to analyse individual areas and tasks pursuant to a minister's approval. It is of even less legal validity --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. Before we get to that, I -- really, what I want to find out is whether or not over the years, 1997, 1998, 1999, the minister of interior and the deputy minister kept making orders establishing a staff which were impossible to implement. So I just want to know if you're saying if this one also was impossible to implement.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to be able to convey to you something that I'm absolutely certain of as an expert who dealt with the police in a professional manner. If we analyse this document we can see that it was made on the 15th of May, 1998, approximately one month after the decision by the minister. This decision was made by the chief of the SUP. There is another decision one month prior to that made by the chief of the sector --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I hear your answer to include a statement that this decision is made by the chief of the SUP. You may be --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, the chief of the public security sector, that's the person who signed the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, before you --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the person before the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think question I'm asking you is capable of a yes, affirmative, or no, negative, answer. Is this document --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you put a specific question, I'll answer it with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was impossible to implement, this order of June 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have in mind the decision made by the chief of the sector, Djordjevic? I don't see the date. I think it was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. 15th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Isn't it clear that a month later there was, or rather, that this decision was a month later than the original one. Had it not been for the first one, this would not have been able to be implemented. The situation is getting more complex, the paper trail can longer no reflect the situation in the field, and that's it, that's the essence. Legal norms should be viewed within the social context. Three decisions are made within a single month and it is a clear indication that papers could not resolve the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Law requires normative analysis, formal analysis --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You know, I really am not understanding what you are saying. Are you saying there is no point in looking at these orders, paper doesn't -- the orders made by the minister and by the chief of the public security department don't matter?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me, please, whether or not this is your opinion that this order before you was also impossible to implement?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proof that it could not is that there another decision made a month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. So your answer is no. Let's just look at the one made a month later. This is P1505, which is what you deal with in -- at page 85 in English, page 149 in B/C/S, of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour, Mr. Stamp I believe is misstating the testimony of the witness when he says your answer is no. When the question is: Was it also impossible? I believe the answer of the witness was yes and it's [indiscernible] based on the fact that there was a second one a month later. So I think Mr. Stamp is misstating the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I disagree with you, Mr. Ivetic; I agree with Mr. Stamp. But since you highlight confusion perhaps we can go back to the witness and see if he will give a simple, straightforward answer to a simple, straightforward question. Was P1251 as at the date it was passes impossible to implement, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the document passed in May by the chief of the sector?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the one. No, because a month later another document was passed. Had the first one been able to be implemented the other one would have been necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the answer is no, Mr. Ivetic. Are we agreed on that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I belive not still, Your Honour. When the answer is saying was is it impossible, and he's saying that it could not be implemented, that means that it is impossible. I mean in Serbian it is very clear. I don't see how to simplify things any further. He's been very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just read the sentence. Had the first one been able to be implemented the other one would have been, and I think the answer was unnecessarily, has been translated as necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Unnecessary, correct. So the answer is that, Yes, it was impossible. It again goes to the original question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's what Mr. Stamp was reflecting in his --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You said the answer was, No, there was no impossible. That is why I rose to my feet because I think now that we're on the same page that's the answer of the witness but at line number 20 Mr. Stamp interpreted this same answer as being no that it was not impossible. That is a very clear issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was not possible, but I think we're on the same page, we understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Simonovic, when you're asked to give a yes or no answer, and that is possible, please do so because counsel can ask you supplementary questions to clarify the situation. Now, Mr. Stamp, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So we get back to P1505, the minister's order of the 16th of June 1998. And I'd like you to look at paragraph 6 thereof. He revokes the order I just showed you and goes on or -- and also re-establishes the staff. Now, if you look at the first sentence after he names the members of the staff, he says: "The expanded staff shall also include chiefs of the secretariats for internal affairs. And branches of the RDB, RDB in the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija." Will you agree with me -- would you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just be patient, Mr. Simonovic, a question will be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the chief of the public sector department, the RJB, would not have been empowered to expand the role of the staff to include RDB, that is something that the minister himself would need to do?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is clear, you are right. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, would you agree -- I think you have said so in you report that the fundamental difference between this order and the previous one is that it expanded the role of the MUP staff Pristina to include the RDB?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Want an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if -- is that something you agree with, that the effect of this would be to expand the role of the MUP staff to include the RDB?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, again we're going back to the rules, but it is necessary to change the rules. But if we look at this decision and if we analyse the decision it's quite clear. See, it is called the decision to establish a ministerial staff for the suppression of terrorism; that is to say that it has a broader name than the other decisions. Now, if we were to carry out an analysis we would have to agree that in order to suppress terrorism successfully it is necessary to establish a level of cooperation between the RDB and the RJB since terrorism is followed through the RDB and the RJB. That is generally known. Therefore, this name, the name of this decision is so broad. However, let's look at it this way. We can look at it systematically and formally. If we were to look at this -- are you following me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, but I think you have answered --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was really asked you about the expansion of the responsibilities of the staff to include the RDB, and I think you agree with me that that would require the intervention of the minister. Can we look at P1811 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before going on. Do you accept that the document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- do you accept that the document in June revoked the one in May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sure, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we look at 1811 quickly, it's 31 May 1999, an order of the minister on the establishment on the staff. And I think you -- not I think. You said at page 157 -- 151 of your report, page 86, second paragraph of the English in respect to this document, P1811, which I think is there before you, that the tasks set out remains unchanged from the previous decree. The question is: Are you saying again that as late as May 1999 the minister was still issuing these orders which were impossible to implement?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents show that attempts were made through paperwork, the form, but the situation was so complex that the ministry could not deal with the problem of terrorism, only within or with its own system. That's why in June 1998 at the Supreme Defence Council a decision was made that five-stage plans on the suppression of terrorism should be put into practice. The minister did not know of that session and that decision of the Supreme Defence Council at the moment when he passed the act of the 16th of June. When the decision was made by the Supreme Defence Council, this being the highest legal act, it could no longer be implemented because a plan adopted at a higher level was supposed to be implemented, the five-stage plan, which also envisaged attempts at coordination and joint action on the part of the ministry -- the police and the army in Kosovo at the time. This was another reason due to which the problem of terrorism in Kosovo could not only be resolved through the activities of the Ministry of the Interior and its staff. It contributed further to the argument, stating that the individual decision which was analysed here could not be implemented in practice because other norms and activities were underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- the question you were asked was about May 1999. What's this answer got to do with the situation in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour. There's no dilemma. This decision that was made in May 1999, it simply copied the tasks that had been adopted a year before that. They could not have been applied then, a year earlier, and they couldn't be applied earlier because the system was -- now what else is interesting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if in 1999 this was still happening how could something have done by the Supreme Defence Council in 1998 explain any of it, including what was happening in 1998 as well as 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1999, in May, it's the 31st of May, what is underway is the bombing of Serbia, NATO is bombing Serbia; and what happened happened. So by virtue of that fact, legal perfectionism could not be enforced, I mean that is my explanation for this kind of thing. There is yet another matter there that is of interest. The tasks of the staff are completely the same, in the decision from a year before that and this one from May 1999. However, the composition of the staff is not the same. My understanding, as I studied the subject, was that the professional structure of the officers involved was not the same. So the question is: How can you simply copy the same tasks for people who belong to a different kind of police profession or different kinds? There is another thing we haven't mentioned. In order to implement some voluminous and complex tasks, irrespective of the system of organization of legal norms, as far as I can see here and as far as I managed to understand -- I beg your pardon. On the basis of this entire case, on this staff there was always between 7 and 12 people. Do you think that 7 or 12 people can do all of those things that were placed under their jurisdiction? There is another thing that can be looked at as a counterpart. The provincial secretariat of the MUP had about 1.000 people, a personnel of 1.000. I don't know about the staff of the Pristina Corps. And to give such tasks to seven men, I mean really, the only explanation I can give is that paper can take anything. I'm an expert, I am trying to go into the core of the matter, to use this logic to the very end, to have the Court see it that way, and I want that with all my heart because it is crystal clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Logic won't answer the problems that are posed by these documents, Professor. We need to get to the heart of the matter and that's where expertise is usually of particular assistance. Anyway, we will develop that in the afternoon. It's now time to break again. That break will be for an hour, so would you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Professor, you said in your evidence and in your report that the authority to deploy the special police units, in particular the PJP, was vested in the minister of interior or his duly appointed designate. And you also said - let me go straight to it - at page 150 of your report in B/C/S, page 86 in English, first paragraph of page 86 in English, and I could just read the part I want to focus on. "In other words, the minister assigned the staff only with specific tasks from the scope of his own authorisations. He also kept all these authorisations. He delegated them to the staff but did not transfer them to the staff. The minister could not reduce the ministerial power that pursuant to the constitution and law belongs to the minister." Now, is there any law you're aware of that prevented the minister from delegating to the staff - to use your word, delegate - the authority to deploy the PJP?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood your question, the minister wasn't absolutely free to do so, he must behave within the frameworks of the authorisations prescribed governing the interior functioning of the MUP. The minister had the right to bring in the rules, but the rules had to be adopted by the government and the government could change it. So ministerial authority was restricted in that sense. He is only a part of the government. He cannot add -- act outside of the policy of his government or change arbitrarily the rules or transfer authority to others. I can stipulate the laws that bear that out if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say the minister delegate his -- certain authorisations to the staff, what authorisations did he delegate to the staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we analyse what he delegated to the staff, then we have to start out from looking at what he could realistically designate to the staff, what it was in realistic terms that the staff could do, bearing in mind the decision and bearing in mind what could be realistically put into practice. So it's only in the field of information that the staff was able to be part of an auxiliary link in the chain, but not more than that. The staff could not bring in decisions, plan, organize, manage, that was within the frameworks of another system. So, in fact, the minister could not designate that to someone else without changing the rules and to change the rules the government had to approve this, so that's the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This -- you asked a simple question, Mr. Stamp. Are you departing from that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you're not then perhaps you would ask it again and ask the witness to answer it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you clearly and simply just tell us what authorisations you are speaking of that were delegated by the minister to the staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- no, that's not what I understood your question to be. Your question related to the PJP. Are you wanting a wider --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- are you wanting to deal with a wider issue or do you want to deal with the PJP?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question I'm dealing with, and I'll get back to the PJP, is in respect to his statement that the minister delegated certain authorisations to the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. But please note that the earlier question about the PJP was not answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you just focus on that. Do you know what or can you tell us simply what authorisations you are referring to here that were delegated to the staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in simple terms, the decisions that could be implemented in practice. So the minister had the idea -- well, of what he wrote, in fact; however, that was not applicable. So where's the problem there? There's another point here. The minister is a political personage, and as a political figure he doesn't need to know the rules governing internal organization, but he has his cabinet, his secretaries that explain that to him and they will say, Mr. Minister this can go ahead, this cannot. So I think we should not blame the minister as a political personage but the secretariat, the cabinet, offices that should have said, Mr. Minister, you cannot do that, you have to change the rules first, and that is no simple matter. So I think that would be the best answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you really don't know of any authorisation that he delegated to the staff? You weren't referring to any specific authorisations when you wrote what I just read from your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't thinking -- well, when I wrote the report I had the organization of the MUP and the system and these decisions and individual decisions, that's what I had at my disposal. So outside that there was nothing, those were my frameworks, my purview, because you have to start out from the system, the legal system defined by the rules. That's the starting point for all considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Going back to the earlier question, what legal provision, do you know of any, that would prevent the minister --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- from designating the chief of the MUP staff as someone who could deploy the SUP -- sorry, the PJPs?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I have to give this some thought, take a while to consider it. What did you say? Did the minister have the right to authorise -- what was it -- some other person, that is to say the chief of a particular department, to be in command of the PJP. Was that your question is that what you were asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Today you were shown two documents in which the minister established these special police units, the PJP, and you were asked who could deploy them and you referred to the documents and said the minister could or somebody duly authorised by him could deploy them. I'm asking you what would have stopped him, what could have prevented him, from giving that authority to the chief of the MUP staff Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm trying to -- well, I seem to be understanding your question better now. This is the matter in hand. The PJP was established on the basis of an individual decision, and the MUP staff was also established on the basis of an individual decision; however, the organization of the MUP, something I talked about in response to questions from the Defence counsel, was a system at a higher level and the rules governing internal organization. So the minister couldn't designate more authorities to the staff without taking away some authority from someone else beforehand. So that is the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- so do you know of any provision or any rule that stopped the minister from designating -- from designating the chief of the MUP staff Kosovo as somebody who could deploy the PJP and the other special police units?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something that was absolutely certain was that he had to change the rules, and the rules are above the minister because they were adopted by the government. So that's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp pointed out to you that this morning you said the minister could command the PJP or he could authorise someone to command the PJP. You agree with that, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, why could the minister not authorise Mr. Lukic to command the PJP is the question. Never mind whether he's the head of the MUP staff for Kosovo or anywhere else. Why could he not nominate Mr. Lukic to command the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question now. He could nominate Mr. Lukic to command the PJP but there had to be a decision whereby he was appointing him, nominating him a commander, otherwise it could have been some other person. So there must be a decision whereby a police official is nominated commander of the PJP in conformity with the staff specifications within the ministry. But as far as I know, this wasn't the decision. He appointed him as being Chief of Staff, where this other matter was regulated by the rules and the decision on establishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it not possible that the special police units, including the PJP, had a dual responsibility to their commander as well as to the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the provisions that I studied which represent the basis, the groundwork, for formulating the Ministry of the Interior, certainly there was no dual command, that is to say in the police there is no term "command," but organization and management. So under management it was under the police administration and the PJP commander. So that job position was defined in that way on the basis of the staffing specifications, which means that Mr. Lukic wasn't appointed as being commander of the PJP, he was appointed to another function. So that Mr. Lukic didn't have authorisation and authority to exert command over something that was not defined by the minister unless a separate decision was taken, and I don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Lukic when asked about the operations of the MUP staff vis-a-vis the PJPs -- and Mr. Lukic actually I should say, he said, and I quote: "The special police units, PJP, had dual responsibility, one to the commander of the PJP units and the other to the Chief of Staff." Just for the record that's P948 at page 53. Now, having regard to that statement by General Lukic I ask you again: Is it not possible that there could be dual responsibility for the work of the PJP vested in its commander and also the chairman of the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, things are quite clear to me. Legally looking at the matter there could not have been a dual command unless regulated by the system. But the fact that Mr. -- what General Lukic said, who is Mr. Lukic today, what he said, well that's easily explained to me. It is a matter of psychology. Do you want me to go on and explain or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- is what I've said enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to explain it and go into the whole story into the matter. Well, there's something that's quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... briefly and clearly, what in it is a matter of psychology why he would say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, reading many statements given by many people that he met, I understood it that they wished to attributed greater -- to boost their image more than the system allowed them, and then they were either unsuccessful or they told some stories which legally speaking don't stand from the aspects of the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who told stories?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, studying the documents that I had access to in preparing for my testimony in the various minutes, records, and so on, I saw that individual officers and policemen made certain statements which were not in harmony with the legal system, lending themselves more weight than the law would allow for, and then there was certain statements that I came across, which legally speaking don't have any coverage in the law and the system of organization within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that what you are saying General Lukic --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're attributing that attitude to Mr. Lukic. Have you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Me? You're asking me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps two or three times I happened to be in the same room with Mr. Lukic, after the year 2000 when for some six months or maybe a little longer I happened to work in the MUP in a working group for the reform of the police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did -- have you met him also here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I just saw him in 2000 at a couple of meetings where I was one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you have access to the record of his interview by the Prosecution here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I did not, I did not read that interview, no. I did not read the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Obrad Stevanovic testified in the Milosevic case that he was not in charge of the PJP in 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, were you shown or were you aware that he said that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no -- that he said what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That he was not in charge of the PJP in 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear any statement to that effect, either statement, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be allowed to say something and try and help you out, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you can tell us who was the commander of the PJP in 1999 that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not know who was the commander in 1992 [sic], perhaps it was Obrad Stevanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't know why it came over as 1992. I said 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
