utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise, I misspoke, 1999. But there's something else that I seem to feel is important here in this context. May I be allowed to say what that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear what you think is important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion what is important is this. It doesn't matter whether, for example, Lukic or Obrad Stevanovic was the commander in 1999, that is easily established on a basis of the analysis of the system and all the rest of it. The substance of the matter is that the problems took place in the base, the base, that is in the implementation of specific actions which were based on principles just like in these proceedings. So it doesn't matter who was in command. What I believe is important is the following, whether the person in command ordered certain things which would be unacceptable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are matters for us and not for you, with respect, Professor. But since you say that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I apologise then, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- it is easily established on an analysis of the system who was in command of the PJP, why is it you can't tell us the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, as far as I know it is a generally known fact that General Obrad Stevanovic was commander of the PJP, as far as I know. Again, I'm just saying, I really have to say that I haven't seen his documents, I haven't seen his decision of appointment, but as a lawyer, since I don't know that, since I haven't seen the decision on his appointment, I should say that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In preparing your report were you not concerned to identify who was in command of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to be quite frank, what I was trying to do was to understand the essence of the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior and to link that up to the analysis of the functioning of the system at a higher level. The system, the constitution, I thought that was more important, I thought that was my basic task, not what individual was in which individual position. It was important for me to see how positions functioned, not what persons were in what positions. You can establish these matters of fact if you are interested in them. I was interested in the processes, in the legality of it, the authority vested in ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we hope for from experts is that they are so steeped in their subject that they don't need to go into a study of the detailed provisions, they're so familiar with them that they can then look more broadly at the way in which these were operating in a particular situation and express their opinion. That's why you're being asked these questions that you don't seem to have an answer to. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know you have said that you didn't see or you weren't told about what General Obradovic said -- General Stevanovic said, General Obrad Stevanovic said, but you have offered an explanation as to why Mr. Lukic said what he said. Do you have any opinion as to why General Stevanovic would deny that he was commander or in charge of the PJP in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- first of all, he never read his statement, it was presented partially to this witness and he should speculate definitely at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, he should, there's a word missing I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He would definitely speculate if he answers this question, why General Stevanovic would deny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stamp, is there likely to be an answer that could be more than speculation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think he, as an expert, is capable of saying whether or not he can offer an opinion based on what he knows about the circumstances surrounding the command of the PJP or whether or not he would need to speculate in terms of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Simonovic, bearing in mind that you do have a belief at least about who was the commander of the PJP, do you consider yourself able to express an opinion as to why General Stevanovic would deny in his evidence here on oath in another case that he was the commander of the PJP in 1999? And if you feel you cannot express an opinion, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot answer that question because it goes beyond my framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring back 1D680. The document that you were asked about by both Mr. Lukic and also the Court, and while it's coming up can I ask you: How many ranks are there in the police force more senior to lieutenant-general, the rank to which general -- or Mr. Lukic was promoted to in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure about the answer, but I think that there is no higher rank than colonel-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, in making -- in making or reporting on the Law of Ranks, is that something that you as an expert should be familiar with, what are the available ranks to which General Lukic could be promoted?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if General Lukic was a major-general, is that right, then he could only have been promoted one rank up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At page 44 of your report you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where in the hierarchy does the rank lieutenant-general come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these are ranks of general, so it is ranks that were given within the Ministry of the Interior. There are no other ranks. So General Lukic, at that time General Lukic, had one of these ranks of general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Stamp. It would appear the witness does not know the ranks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a university professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. And, Professor, the first time you have really written about the MUP staff - am I not right - or done a study on the MUP staff specifically is this report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote this report that is in front of us when I was asked by the Defence lawyers to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer the question you've been asked. Listen carefully and answer the question. Is this the first time you've written a study on the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the first time that I wrote a study on the MUP staff, but before that I wrote studies about the police system in Serbia, and I dealt with that. The MUP staff is just part of the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what have you written beyond the subject of community policing about the operation of the police in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote a large number of papers that deal with different aspects of community policing and also aspects of traditional policing and police work, and in addition to that I dealt with the application of crime methods and other fields of criminal law. I wrote a textbook called: "Criminal Science."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we're not studying in this particular situation criminal law or criminalistics. We are studying administrative law at the moment. Now, is that a field in which you claim expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My special field is -- well, I've been dealing with the police, and within that the organization of the police, and the organization of the police cannot be researched without analysing the organization of government and constitutional law. And that is why I started from an analysis of constitutional law and then administrative law and then I came to the legal provisions regarding the police. Perhaps that's why it's as voluminous as it is. So we're going back to the subject that we started dealing with yesterday. In order to understand the police you have to understand administrative law and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just ask the question again without -- please listen to it. Have you written any study devoted specifically to the structure of the police in Kosovo before this report?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just look at -- if we could move on, page 48 of your report, which is page 80, I think, in B/C/S, 48 in English. This is the last question on this. You said at the end of the section, which is the first paragraph of page 48, that Mr. Lukic's direct superior when he was in Belgrade held the rank of major, two ranks below the rank of major-general. What are the ranks between major and major-general?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above major there is lieutenant-colonel, then colonel, then major-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So you would agree with me that it should be three ranks below?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, esteemed colleague, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have the law there in front of you where the -- I think I see where the various ranks are set out; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, not in front of me but inter alia I studied the Law on Ranks in the Ministry of the Interior. I don't have it right in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you have in front of you this document that you were shown earlier by learned counsel and you were asked about the last paragraph, in which you said it was unnecessary. But my question is this: In making a recommendation for a promotion to one of the higher ranks of general, does the minister not have an obligation to set out the reasons why he makes the recommendation?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question, it is fully clear to me. Since this was a regular promotion -- I never wrote a document on promotion, sir, but as far as regular promotion is concerned I assume that the head of state has to trust the minister and his proposal. Now let us go to a legal level in general terms. Every decision has to have a rationale, that is a general, legal principle, a principle of law, isn't it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just -- but you could tell me quickly. I mean, I don't want to spend too long on this. Is the minister obliged to give reasons on -- in making his recommendation?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the law does not stipulate that, especially when it is a regular promotion, and this was a regular promotion. However, the question can be put in this way, of legal technical perfectionism. In that case there should be reasons provided, but certainly not this way, bearing in mind what it was that we had discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now -- well, you see the reasons the minister has given, that in the past year Lukic has excelled in successful command and control of MUP units engaged in the prevention of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija. Is it your evidence that the minister was deliberately misrepresenting to the president the role of Mr. Lukic in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am just claiming that what that statement of reasons says could not have been correct in view of the entire story that is derived from the very logic of things and my expertise, or rather, I tried to catch this logic of the law and the rules because -- I mean, he did not have that authority. The system was different. Why the minister wrote that when he sent a letter, this letter, to the president of the country I really cannot say. In my view that would not be right. But on the other hand the legal requirements were met for the promotion, it is a regular promotion, not an extraordinary one, the occasion was there, the police holiday, it was a war situation that needed a boost of morale, if I understood things properly, and as many decorations as possible needed to be handed out and that would be about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on to another topic. You wrote a little bit paramilitaries. Were you made aware of evidence that a paramilitary volunteer group called the Skorpions was incorporated into the reserves of the SAJ in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I could not give a meritorious answer to that question. The only thing I know is that the SAJ was established in accordance with the law, and the only thing I know is that in the police there were no paramilitary units. It is so regulated by law. I am not sufficiently familiar with this specific case in order to give a proper answer, it would involve speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But if there was this group, the paramilitary group Skorpions, incorporated in the SAJ, would it not mean that in many cases the law was floated by those in command of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask for counsel, since he said about evidence, I'd like to find out what evidence that is. If he could cite to the evidence because the only one I remember is Mr. Stoparic, who came here and said he was a former member of the Skorpions and reservist of the police. What evidence is Mr. Stamp talking about here, I don't recall any on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The evidence of Goran Stoparic, both in testimony and --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: His witness statement says former members of the Skorpions and in his testimony here he said he was a reservist of the police and is proud of that fact. So I would like to see the exact reference that you're referring to when you cite something as grandiose as stating that a group, a paramilitary group, the Skorpions was incorporated into the SAJ. Where is that positive evidence in this record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a broader issue here, Mr. Stamp, which is the witness has said that there were no paramilitary units in the police. Now, it's -- is it not possible for you to ask the question whether the acceptance of any would therefore amount to a flagrant breach of the regulations without getting personal on this particular topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would respectfully put the question in precise terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wouldn't the acceptance of paramilitary groups or volunteers be a flagrant breach of the law as it was in Kosovo in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, he's gone back to the same issue, as it was in Kosovo 1999 cannot be part of this question. It's the same objectionable question as the last one. He can ask the first part of it but not the last part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We repel that objection. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You heard the question, professor, can you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The system of legal norms and regulations regulating the work of the police did not envisage any inclusion of paramilitary units into the police system. When it comes to volunteers, they could be included into larger units in the sense of volunteer units. As for the Skorpions, I cannot tell you anything precisely because I'm not familiar with the facts; however, I'm absolutely positive that the legal regulation regulating the conduct of the police only envisaged inclusions of police members who are either active-duty officers or reserve police officers and no one else. That's what I can tell you as to your question. The rest would be in the realm of speculation and I suppose this is the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you can avoid answering the question. What you say about volunteers is consistent with a great deal of evidence we've had here, but the question also extended to paramilitary units and you say that the regulations did not envisage the inclusion of paramilitary units. The question, however, is whether the inclusion of any paramilitary unit would be contrary to the laws governing the operation of the MUP. Now, what is the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is clear. Including paramilitary units would be against the regulation that existed in the MUP at the time regulating the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior. Such regulation did not envisage that paramilitary units can be included, only the reserve police force was referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of a provision that enables the police authorities to include or recruit volunteers into the police force -- volunteer units I should ask.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law envisages that the reserve force of the Ministry of the Interior can be utilised, it is prescribed in the Law on Internal Affairs, Article 28 as well as 27, that's what the law says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I should have made it clear -- in fact, I may have misrepresented the evidence earlier. The evidence in the case indicates that volunteers were accepted into, in the general term, Serb forces. It would be wrong of me to say there was much evidence in relation to the police on that subject because I can't remember. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at page 44 of the statement, and I wish to ask just two questions about what you said in regard to ID cards -- sorry, it's page 74 in your copy, and I am directing you to the part in the vicinity of footnote 254 and this is page 44 in the English. You said: "The law -- or the 1996 law on Yugoslav citizens' passports modernised this provision ..." So the first question I want to ask you, isn't it the Law on Travel Documents you are talking about? Do you know of a law on Yugoslav citizens' passports?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with that law. Concerning that issue the essence is that the identity card --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before we get to that, what is the law called? Isn't it called -- and I just want to know for the record, isn't it called the Law on Travel Documents? Could we bring P1833 --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, your answer is yes. So it's not the law on Yugoslav citizens' passports, it's the Law on Travel Documents?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Law on Travel Documents of Yugoslav citizens, that's the title of the law in the Official Gazette published in Belgrade, 1996, the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene. Now, we've heard of this even earlier. Does it also include laws on passport or travel documents would be different? I think I need a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From me, Your Honour, or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Travel documents include passports; however, there were also identity cards. The essence is that the constitution of both the FRY and Serbia states that the citizens are guaranteed the freedom to move and leave the Republic of Serbia -- excuse me, being in possession of a travel document or identity card was not a precondition used to determine whether one is a Yugoslav citizen or not. The proof of citizenship lay with a number of other documents, such as the birth registers, citizens registers, marriage registers, and based on those travel documents, passports, and identity cards were issued. The basic documents are the citizens registers as well as birth registers. If one possesses an identity card or a passport or if those were taken away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I was just trying to find out the law on the travel documents because there are documents for travelling purposes to the neighbouring countries where you don't need a passport. Does that law include that as well and it also includes the passport -- that is where it also includes the passport or the passport has a separate law and travel document law is different? That's the only thing I wanted for my own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the answer to your question because I am from Negotin which is a border town in Serbia. In addition to the passport we also had permissions to cross borders and move in the border belt between two states. These were licences, permissions, not passports per se. And this covered the entire border area of the former FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... passports plus those documents, this is the only thing you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So the Law on Travel Documents you said enabled Yugoslav citizens to cross the border even if they didn't have travel documents. And you said: "The only obligation was to verify whether the person was a Yugoslav citizen or not." So the question is this --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say so. I said that when one is entering a country, being in possession of a passport was not a precondition to be able to enter. They could prove in other ways that they were Yugoslav or Serbian citizens, or rather, the FRY at the time. When leaving the country under the then-law they had to show a passport or the licence to move in the border belt in order to leave the country. That is what the law envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, look at your report at page 1 -- page 74 in B/C/S, page 44 in English, at footnote 254. I'll read it. "In other words, the 1996 Law on Travel Documents," which is what it should be, "modernises provisions so that any Yugoslav citizen has the right to leave and return to the country at any time, irrespective of the fact that he/she does not have a passport when crossing the border. Of course the only obligation was to verify as to whether the person was a Yugoslav citizen or not." The question is simply this: If people were forced -- well, let's use a neutral word. If masses of people left the country for a different reason, would it not be at least helpful in proving their identity and that they were Yugoslav citizens if they had ID cards so that they could return?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the identity card is only used for internal processes and in order to prove one's identity. It is not the passport that is used for that. The only document used to prove one's identity when leaving the country and spending time abroad as well as enjoying certain rights with our embassies and missions was the passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but you are saying the passport was not necessary to cross the border. I'm just asking you this simply. If a Yugoslav citizen wanted to return to the country and needed to prove that he was a Yugoslav citizen and also prove his identity, wouldn't an ID card help?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I don't need to go to that article since the answer is clear, but it says here that citizens can enter the country but only after his or her identity has been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to establish that person's identity an ID card would be of assistance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that is not the only way. We have the citizens registers, birth registers, those were the basic documents, and the documents you are referring to are issued against those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you mean to say that a Yugoslav citizen could leave and return to the country at any time without -- even without a passport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The law regulated it in such a way that a Yugoslav citizen when leaving a country needs to show his or her passport. Exceptionally Yugoslav citizens can enter the country even without a passport --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the legislator had in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that case we better get you to read a sentence from your report. Now, in the paragraph in front of you in English it's maybe 15 or 16 lines into the paragraph and it's -- the sentence says: "In other words, the 1996 law on Yugoslav citizens' passports modernised this provision ..." Now, can you read that sentence aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me locate that first, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The sentence ends with footnote 254.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the page on the screen. You'll see footnote 254 at the very top of the screen. So we need to come down the page a little --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see 254 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh we need to go back to page 73, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's 74 in his copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but I think we need to go back one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, right, 73 to 74.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can we go back. Now would you read the sentence that begins on the second-last line I think on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the wrong page, it's 482, we have to have 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the top of the page I think it should be number 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 73. Now, go to the very bottom. Right. Now, could you read the last sentence on that page, please, read it aloud -- on the screen -- just look at the screen, please -- Mr. Simonovic, please look at the screen in front of you. Read the last sentence at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. "In other words, the Law on Travel Documents of Yugoslav citizens of 1996 modernised this provision in the sense that every person who was a Yugoslav citizen had the right at any moment to leave the country and return into the country" -- now I have to move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, and read the next -- the beginning of the next page, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, we've gone a page too far. There we are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. " -- and to return to the country irrespective of the fact that at the moment when crossing the border he or she was not in possession of a travel document." I understand the question. One thing is indisputable here. According to the regulations and in my experience, this citizen would have to show a passport when leaving the country. When returning to the country, he or she would be allowed into the country even without a passport if they can prove that they are Yugoslav citizens or, that is, the citizens of the FRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're saying that in practice this law was not observed; is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm trying to say that the citizen under law when leaving the country had to show a passport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's not what the sentence says, that's not what you're sentence telling us what the law is says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The rationale of the text was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Never mind the rationale. Just tell us whether you've read it accurately -- you've understood it accurately or have you made a mistake in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want to say this, the citizen under the then-regulation and the current regulation had to show a travel document not an ID, when leaving the country. When entering the country they need to show a travel document; if they don't have one, they can prove what their identity is by other means in order to gain access to the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you agreed with me that one means would be the ID card. You said at the beginning of page 75 of the statement, same -- the same -- page 44 in the English version, that these ID cards were technologically obsolete and of little use. If that is the case can I ask you why it is that the president of Serbia in the crisis of a war passed a law widening the scope of application of the Law on ID cards, lowering the age for mandatory possession of ID cards?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed colleague, Mr. Stamp, in order to answer your question I would probably have to speculate as to why at the time -- I presume that provision -- or rather, the Law on Identity Cards during the time of war was put into force in order to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, if you need to speculate, let's abandon that question. You wrote a lot in the beginning of your report about -- about the president of the Serbia and the role and responsibilities of the president of Serbia. Are you holding out yourself to be an expert on the constitutional law of Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed colleague, Mr. Prosecutor, I do not believe myself to be an expert in constitutional law --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that area should be covered by my esteemed colleague Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Therefore, I will not ask you any questions about that. When I look at your CV there is one thing I wanted to ask you. You have in it that you wrote a paper on tactical ways of gaining -- of confession by strategy by relevant influence on emotions. Do you know if that paper is available in English?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed colleague, can you refer to the exact title of the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think I just did, this is 6D669, that is your curriculum vitae, and in e-court it's page 5, and it says here in English that you published a paper entitled: "Tactical ways of gaining of confession by strategy of relevant influence on emotions ." Do you know where one could find a copy of that paper in English?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed colleague, unfortunately there is no translation in English, but I am ready to have it translated at my expense and forwarded to you by mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does the paper concern? There are different tactics of gaining confessions and influencing emotions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will ask Mr. Lukic to follow-up on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's another one on gaining a confession based on artfulness, Mr. Stamp, perhaps you might wish that one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Those papers are not in English you said?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have it in English, but I can send it to you. These are strategies used all over the world in criminal science. I cited the procedures and rules used by the police when using different methods to gain confessions. They are used by all police forces of the world in the United States, in -- by your police, in Serbia as well, and as a professor of criminal science that is what my research was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, esteemed colleague, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have re-examination, Mr. Lukic, do you? Not at the moment, but do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We also have some questions. Just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask if it is possible - this is a question for the interpreters - whether it is possible to continue for about -- it could be anything up to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters say yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. If we do that, Judge Chowhan cannot stay with us because of urgent personal reasons, and therefore we will retire just now and we will return shortly to the bench. Just, please, everyone stay where they are while we re-arrange the court. --- Break taken at 3.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, Professor. The first of these relates to an early part of your report, in English it's page 26, it's immediately after a heading: "Position of internal affairs organs in the country's defence system."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I could maybe it's page 42 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- on his copy, and I don't know perhaps a reference to the footnote might also help him to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, there isn't -- but it's immediately before footnote 165. Now, if -- we recognise that you do not hold yourself out as an expert in constitutional law, but at the beginning of that section you say: "After the Law on Defence had come into effect competent federal organs took over the activities performed by defence organs in member republic" -- do you have it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Bonomy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say that: "After the Law on Defence had come into effect competent federal organs took over the activities performed by defence organs in member republics," and you say then, "in the Republic of Serbia pursuant to the Law on Defence they were performed by organs of the Republic of Serbia." Now, my question for you is this: Are you saying that the Republic of Serbia actually had a Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This is the way it was. The Republic of Serbia did not have a Ministry of Defence. A ministry -- the Ministry of Defence was abolished through this decision on ministries but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but between 1991 and the passing of the FRY constitution in 1992, was there, in fact, a Ministry of Defence? Simple question, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, abolished later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did it do?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Ministry of Defence at that time dealt with all matters related to defence, but then this field of work moved on to federal level. So in this observed period in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia there was no Ministry of Defence that it was at the level of the member republics. There is only the Federal Ministry of Defence governed by the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So during that period did the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia have responsibilities in relation to the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was it that you said, the Ministry of Defence -- no, no, no. That's never the way it was in that system. This goes beyond -- I mean if I can put it that way, beyond my police expert knowledge. But, as far as I know it was always the federal organs that were in charge of the army, always. As far as the republican level probably there was some jurisdiction in terms of territorial defence -- or rather, the area organs that later on moved on to the Federal Ministry of Defence. But as I've been saying to you, I'm not an expert in these fields, so I wouldn't dare -- it does not include the period of my research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But one of the things you do in this document is highlight, as we have already had highlighted in the case, the fairly modest role that the constitution gave to the president of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the way this role was realistically Professor Ratko Markovic explained that very well in his report -- I can elaborate on that, but I guess there's no need to. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I want to ask you a specific question. Why or how -- I think is the question. How was it that Slobodan Milosevic came to be so powerful when he was president of the Republic of Serbia if the president's powers are as limited as you say?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a field of constitutional law and it's a political question. I cannot respond to that question, I cannot give an expert's response, I cannot even answer it as a lawyer, and I really wouldn't want to make a mistake and I wouldn't want to be saying things I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you dispute that between 1992 and 1997 he was a very powerful man in the Republic of Serbia and, indeed, in Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not disputing that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said something about the border police. They were, in your evidence and indeed in other evidence we've had, answerable to the border police administration in the Ministry of the Interior in Belgrade. Why is it that controlling the border of Yugoslavia was not a federal function?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a question that is better put to a constitutional law expert than to me, but I think that the question is quite logical. But I'm not an expert in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 was there a Federal Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this ministry did exist but its authority was not such that it could significantly affect the work of the police at that time in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I did not deal with this question. I tried to go into the essence of police work in Serbia. I know that they dealt in international cooperation, cooperation with Interpol and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you inquire into who -- or, sorry, how the members of the MUP staff were paid while they were serving on the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot answer that question. There were many witnesses who were on that MUP staff who could have answered that question much better than I can because they were members of that staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your report is 6D668. You've had it before you while giving your evidence. As a result of the questions that you've been asked so far, is there any element or aspect of your report that you wish to alter?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood your question, Your Honour. Perhaps if I were to change something in this report, I think that the sentence that we discussed a few moments ago is not very precise when I said that somebody could leave the country and come back without documents. As far as I know, he or she has to show a document before leaving the country. When entering the document one has to show -- I beg your pardon, a passport. So there is this exceptional possibility of someone entering the country even without a passport because possession of a passport and possession of a personal identity card is not a constituent part of the citizenship of Serbia. What was attempted through this law was to go into the essence of the matter, not to have it reduced to paperwork. That is what we discussed and then I realized that that was a weakness, or rather, I realized that the wording was not right and that it was not clear enough. Your Honour, I'm quite sure that the basis of this report, the basis of this report -- I mean, what I'm trying to say is all the basic things are right because I studied the system of organization for a long time, and I really stand by this expert opinion of mine with regard to all the questions that we discussed today, the system, organization, planning, and so on, I really stand by that. I tried to present my logical evidence during the course of the day today, and I'm sure that that is the truth that I wish to present to this Court with the best of intentions as an expert and without any idea or any wish to have anyone not be answerable for what they did. I tried to be fully logical and I wanted to have maximum cooperation with you on every fact leading to the truth. The truth was primary for me in terms of the realization of these legal norms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything arising from that for you, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very short one, Your Honour. Please can we have P1505 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, this is a decision to establish a ministerial staff, this is the document we began with and we shall conclude with it as well. Let us look at the last page, please. Professor, the last sentence of the last page reads: "Send this decision to the head, deputy head, and members of the staff as well as to the minister's office."

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Going through the exhibits and other documents that were at your disposal, did you ever find any proof that the then-General Sreten Lukic ever received this decision?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I reply? I didn't come across any proof, but I'm wondering what that proof would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move on. What do you mean what proof, what kind of proof?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would probably mean that had he received it, it would have been registered in the log, such as the one we have at the university, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or to sign the decision itself.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of your work, since it says here members of the staff, did you also come across any evidence that any members of the staff got this decision?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV SIMONOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When researching this case --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the -- first of all, to establish relevance for this you'll need to establish what research he carried out into that particular question and then we'll see where we're going. Is this a matter he was asked to research?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just tried and that was everything I had for the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor, thank you for your testimony before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor Simonovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to assist us. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to thank you and your colleagues for your patience and desire to go and analyse the legal regulations referred to in order to arrive at a truth. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're the first one to thank me for my patience, Mr. Simonovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll come tomorrow if you have a witness for us, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour -- yes, Your Honour. We are in constant contact with Mr. Kovacevic, who was here and left because of illness, and we are not able to bring this witness back and even -- we don't want to propose the videolink because his doctor specifically said he cannot testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the only witness we have left is 6D-1, coming on -- tomorrow afternoon, half past 2.00. So we don't have a witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the last witness would be and the only one, 6D-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the estimated time for that would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: An hour and a half to two hours. She will be live because we won't have time to do a statement within the 48-hour rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sepenuk, on the question of handwriting, is there likely to be that evidence next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: We expect three witnesses next week, Your Honour, Dusan Mladenovski, who's a very, very short witness and Dr. Fruits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And Professor Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And Aleksic is a problem, is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, Your Honour. Frankly I don't think there would be time for him in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if they could indicate the order. We are a little bit stretched especially in respect to Dr. Fruits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you asking that he be the last witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you accommodate that, Mr. Sepenuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think we can, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. So 9.00 on Monday in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of April, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
